title: Inquest launched into Port Hope cell death of Darryl Thompson
article: Northumberland Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) are launching an inquest into the Port Hope cell death of Darryl Thompson last August.

"Every time there's a death of a person in custody it's mandatory there be an inquest. It's under the Coroner's Act," said Northumberland OPP Detachment Commander Inspector Doug Borton. "The Coroner's Office has asked the OPP to assist."

The Ontario Special Investigations Unit (SIU) has already cleared the Port Hope Police Service (PHPS) of any wrongdoing. The SIU, which investigates when police are involved in a death or serious injury, closed their investigation in March. They found the cause of Mr. Thompson's death was intoxication with ethanol and hydromorphone.
At approximately 12:20 a.m. on Wednesday, Aug. 20, 2008, a woman who was walking her dog discovered an unconscious man on the sidewalk in front of a residence at 76 Cavan St.
A man living nearby called the Port Hope Police Service. Mr. Thompson was arrested for public intoxication, taken to the Port Hope police station and put in a cell.

Mr. Thompson was found without vital signs in his cell at 11 a.m. on Wednesday, Aug. 20. Emergency medical workers were called to the scene and took him to Northumberland Hills Hospital where he was pronounced dead by the coroner.

SIU investigators interviewed four members of the Port Hope Police Service, two witness officers and two civilians on the desk that night, plus 17 civilian witnesses, including emergency medical response workers, friends and family and people present at the arrest. The investigation concluded there was no criminal wrongdoing by police.
The SIU report will be part of the new inquest into Mr. Thompson's death.
The inquest will go beyond possible criminal charges to consider all the factors in the in-custody death.

"It's all aspects of the cause of death or anything that may be surrounding the cause of death," said Insp. Borton. "The inquest will make an independent public review and there could be recommendations for the future."
The inquest is less about assigning blame than the SIU investigation and more about considering ways to prevent similar cases in the future.
The entire brief of the incident is expected to be ready by September and the inquest could be complete in late 2009.
